Case Study 2: Dengue, Precipitation and Temperature in Northeastern Brazil

Full SINAN-DENGUE + INMET Pipeline | CE, PE, BA, MA | 2015–2022

Dr. Max Anjos

17 September, 2026

Source: vignettes/ec-02-dengue-clima.Rmd
ec-02-dengue-clima.Rmd

Objective

This case study examines how air temperature and accumulated precipitation modulate the weekly incidence of dengue in the four Brazilian Northeastern states with the highest historical disease burden — Ceara (CE), Pernambuco (PE), Bahia (BA) and Maranhao (MA) — over the 2015–2022 period. The final product is a weekly time series of notified cases integrated with 14-day moving averages of climate variables, ready for use in regression models with control for seasonality and trend.

Scientific Context

Dengue is hyperendemic in Brazil, with cyclical epidemics of increasing magnitude observed since the 1990s. The Northeast concentrates episodes of high transmission associated with specific combinations of temperature and precipitation: the optimal temperature for Aedes aegypti development lies between 26°C and 34°C, while temperatures above 36°C reduce vector survival (Brady et al., 2013). Precipitation, in turn, creates and replenishes artificial and natural breeding sites; there is a characteristic time window of approximately 14 days between the peak in rainfall and the peak in notified cases, reflecting the mosquito’s development cycle plus the virus’s extrinsic incubation period (Simons et al., 2016).

The Northeast displays substantial internal climatic heterogeneity: CE and PE have semi-arid climates in the interior (Sertao) with rainfall concentrated in the first half of the year (ITCZ), while the coastal Zona da Mata is more humid and warm year-round. MA has Amazonian influence in the west and an equatorial monsoon regime. This diversity justifies the stratified analysis by state (UF), which climasus4r implements directly via group_by = "uf".

The 14-day moving window strategy (strategy = "moving_window", window = 14) captures the average of the two preceding weeks of temperature and precipitation, which corresponds biologically to the time required for an active breeding site to produce infectious adult mosquitoes after a heavy rain (Bhatt et al., 2013; Tauil, 2002).

Data Used

Source System Variables States (UF) Period
DATASUS SINAN-DENGUE Cases notified by municipality and date of symptom onset CE, PE, BA, MA 2015–2022
INMET Automatic weather stations Air temperature (tair_dry_bulb_c), precipitation (prec_mm) CE, PE, BA, MA 2015–2022
SINAN vs. SIM-DO: SINAN (Notifiable Diseases Information System) records notified cases (incidence), while SIM records deaths (mortality). For a high-incidence, low-lethality disease such as dengue, SINAN is the appropriate system for analyzing transmission and seasonality.

Full Pipeline 

library(climasus4r)

# --- 1. Import and preparation of health data ---
df_saude <- sus_data_import(
  uf     = c("CE", "PE", "BA", "MA"),
  year   = 2015:2022,
  system = "SINAN-DENGUE",
  lang   = "pt"
) |>
  sus_data_clean_encoding(lang = "pt") |>
  sus_data_standardize(lang = "pt") |>
  sus_data_create_variables(
    create_calendar_vars = TRUE,
    create_age_groups    = TRUE,
    lang                 = "pt"
  ) |>
  sus_data_aggregate(
    time_unit = "week",
    group_by  = "uf",
    lang      = "pt"
  )

# --- 2. INMET climate data ---
df_clima <- sus_climate_inmet(
  uf       = c("CE", "PE", "BA", "MA"),
  year     = 2015:2022,
  variable = c("tair_dry_bulb_c", "prec_mm"),
  lang     = "pt"
) |>
  sus_climate_fill_inmet(method = "linear_interp", lang = "pt")

# --- 3. Health + climate integration ---
df_final <- sus_climate_aggregate(
  df_health  = df_saude,
  df_climate = df_clima,
  strategy   = "moving_window",
  window     = 14,
  group_by   = "uf",
  lang       = "pt"
)

Step-by-Step Explanation

sus_data_import() — Import of SINAN-DENGUE microdata

For system = "SINAN-DENGUE", the function downloads the annual files of confirmed and suspected dengue notifications from the DATASUS FTP. Each record includes: date of symptom onset (DT_SIN_PRI), notification date (DT_NOTIFIC), municipality of residence (ID_MUNICIP), final case classification (confirmed/discarded/suspected), confirmation criterion (laboratory/clinical-epidemiological) and serotyping result when available. climasus4r uses DT_SIN_PRI as the reference date for temporal alignment with the climate data, which is more epidemiologically appropriate than the notification date.

sus_data_standardize() — Controlled vocabulary

After standardization, the date column is renamed date (date of symptom onset), the municipality of residence becomes code_muni (6-digit IBGE code), and the n_cases column is created for case counting in the subsequent aggregation. Confirmation status is stored in case_status with levels "confirmed", "suspected" and "discarded".

sus_data_create_variables() — Calendar and demographic variables

With create_calendar_vars = TRUE, the columns epiweek (CDC epidemiological week — essential for alignment with the Ministry of Health’s epidemiological bulletins), year, month, season and day_of_week are created. With create_age_groups = TRUE using the default breaks (0, 5, 15, 30, 60, Inf), the age_group column is created, useful for differential risk analyses by age group.

Epidemiological week: The epidemiological week (EW) is the standard used in all arbovirus bulletins from the Ministry of Health. EW 1 begins on the first Sunday of the year. climasus4r uses the CDC definition (Sunday to Saturday), compatible with the Brazilian standard.

sus_data_aggregate() with time_unit = "week" and group_by = "uf"

Produces the weekly count of cases per state (UF). Weeks with no notified cases receive a zero count, ensuring complete and continuous time series. The resulting n_cases column represents the total number of cases (confirmed + suspected) notified in that state in that epidemiological week.

sus_climate_inmet() — Dry-bulb temperature and precipitation

tair_dry_bulb_c is the air temperature measured by the dry-bulb thermometer — the conventional ambient air temperature, distinct from wet-bulb temperature (which incorporates relative humidity). For dengue studies, dry-bulb temperature is the standard variable used in the literature to model the larval development rate of Aedes aegypti and the virus’s extrinsic incubation period (Brady et al., 2013).

sus_climate_fill_inmet() with method = "linear_interp"

For variables with an approximately continuous distribution (such as temperature), linear interpolation is often sufficient when gaps are short (1–3 consecutive days). For precipitation series with many zeros and long gaps, it may be necessary to use method = "random_forest".

sus_climate_aggregate() with strategy = "moving_window" and window = 14

The moving window strategy calculates the average of the climate variables over the window days preceding each outcome date. With window = 14, the climate value associated with week W is the average of the last 2 weeks (days -14 to -1 relative to the first day of week W). This window captures both the mosquito’s larval development time (7–10 days) and the dengue virus’s extrinsic incubation period (8–12 days at 28°C), totaling approximately 14–21 days between climate exposure and case notification.

Note on temporal alignment: The 14-day window is an approximation. The sensitivity of results to different windows (7, 14, 21 days) should be assessed in the final models. climasus4r facilitates this analysis by running sus_climate_aggregate() multiple times with different values of window.

Expected Output

After running the pipeline, df_final is a climasus_df object with the following main columns:

Column Type Description
date_week Date First day of the epidemiological week
epiweek integer Epidemiological week number (1–53)
uf character State abbreviation (CE, PE, BA, MA)
n_cases integer Dengue cases notified in the week
tair_dry_bulb_c_w14 double Mean air temperature (°C) — 14-day window
prec_mm_w14 double Mean precipitation (mm/day) — 14-day window

Next Steps

With the df_final dataset available, the analyses most commonly used in the dengue environmental epidemiology literature are:

  • Quasi-Poisson GLM with seasonality: quasi-Poisson regression with Fourier terms for annual seasonality and linear time trend. See the Time Series Modeling tutorial.
  • DLNM model for temperature: nonlinear exposure-response function between temperature and incidence, with a lag distribution of 0 to 21 days.
  • Temperature threshold analysis: estimation of the critical temperature threshold above which transmission increases significantly.

References

Bhatt, S., Gething, P. W., Brady, O. J., et al. (2013). The global distribution and burden of dengue. Nature, 496, 504–507.

Brady, O. J., Golding, N., Pigott, D. M., et al. (2013). Global temperature constraints on Aedes aegypti and Ae. albopictus persistence and competence for dengue virus transmission. Parasites & Vectors, 6, 351.

Simons, R. L., Rizzoli, A., Perez-Ramırez, E., et al. (2016). Socioeconomic factors associated with dengue fever: a cross-sectional survey in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. PLoS ONE, 11(9), e0163367.

Tauil, P. L. (2002). Aspectos criticos do controle do dengue no Brasil. Cadernos de Saude Publica, 18(3), 867–871.

Brasil, Ministerio da Saude (2022). SINAN — Sistema de Informacao de Agravos de Notificacao. Brasilia: DATASUS. Available at: https://datasus.saude.gov.br/
